questions.sub: Contractile and Regulatory Proteins of Muscle
questions.q: Which protein forms the thick filaments of the sarcomere and possesses actin-activated ATPase activity in its globular head domain?
options: Myosin II
F-actin
Tropomyosin
Titin
questions.explain: Myosin II is a hexameric motor protein composed of two heavy chains and four light chains; its S1 globular heads bind actin and hydrolyze ATP to generate the power stroke.

open.q: Name the hexameric motor protein that forms the thick filaments of skeletal muscle sarcomeres.

questions.sub: Contractile and Regulatory Proteins of Muscle
questions.q: Which subunit of the troponin complex binds calcium ions released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum to initiate skeletal muscle contraction?
options: Troponin I
Troponin C
Troponin T
Tropomyosin
questions.explain: Troponin C (TnC) binds four Ca2+ ions, inducing a conformational shift in troponin T and troponin I that moves tropomyosin away from the myosin-binding sites on actin.

open.q: Name the specific subunit of the troponin complex that binds calcium ions during striated muscle contraction.

questions.sub: Contractile and Regulatory Proteins of Muscle
questions.q: Which gigantic elastic sarcomeric protein anchors thick myosin filaments to the Z-disc and contributes to passive muscle elasticity?
options: Nebulin
Alpha-actinin
Titin
Desmin
questions.explain: Titin (connectin) is the largest known human polypeptide, spanning from the Z-disc to the M-line to center myosin filaments and provide passive restoring force.

open.q: Name the giant elastic protein that connects thick myosin filaments to the Z-disc in a sarcomere.

questions.sub: Contractile and Regulatory Proteins of Muscle
questions.q: Which protein links the intracellular actin cytoskeleton of skeletal muscle fibers to the extracellular matrix via the sarcolemmal dystroglycan complex, and is absent in Duchenne muscular dystrophy?
options: Utrophin
Spectrin
Vinculin
Dystrophin
questions.explain: Dystrophin anchors intracellular F-actin to transmembrane beta-dystroglycan; its absence causes sarcolemmal tearing during contraction, leading to Duchenne muscular dystrophy.

open.q: Name the subsarcolemmal cytoskeletal protein that is absent in Duchenne muscular dystrophy.

questions.q: During the cross-bridge cycle, which biochemical event directly causes the myosin head to detach from the actin filament?
options: Binding of a fresh ATP to the myosin head
Hydrolysis of ATP into ADP and free phosphate
Release of inorganic phosphate from the myosin head
Binding of calcium ions to troponin C on the thin filament
questions.explain: Binding of fresh ATP to the nucleotide pocket of myosin reduces its affinity for actin, detaching the cross-bridge; subsequent ATP hydrolysis re-cocks the myosin head.

open.q: Which molecular event directly triggers the detachment of the myosin head from actin during the cross-bridge cycle?
accept: Binding of a new ATP molecule

questions.q: What is the biochemical explanation for rigor mortis after death?
options: Excess lactate covalently crosslinks actin and myosin filaments
ATP depletion prevents myosin detachment while calcium leaks from the SR
Postmortem myosin light-chain phosphatase locks the myosin heads
Autolysis of tropomyosin exposes every actin binding site
questions.explain: Without ATP synthesis after death, Ca2+ leaks into the sarcoplasm to expose actin binding sites, and myosin heads remain locked in the rigor conformation on actin because no ATP is available to induce detachment.

open.q: Depletion of which molecule prevents myosin heads from detaching from actin, causing rigor mortis?

questions.q: In skeletal muscle excitation-contraction coupling, how does depolarization of the T-tubule dihydropyridine (DHP) receptor trigger calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum?
options: DHP receptor generates IP3 that opens ER calcium channels
Extracellular calcium entering via DHP channels binds troponin C directly
Mechanical coupling of the DHP receptor to the ryanodine receptor opens SR channels
DHP receptor activates adenylyl cyclase to raise cyclic AMP
questions.explain: In skeletal muscle, the T-tubule L-type Ca2+ channel (DHP receptor) acts as a voltage sensor physically coupled to the sarcoplasmic reticulum ryanodine receptor (RyR1), unlike cardiac muscle which relies on calcium-induced calcium release.

open.q: Name the calcium release channel on the sarcoplasmic reticulum membrane activated during skeletal muscle excitation-contraction coupling.

questions.q: A 16-year-old boy develops severe hyperthermia (41.2 C), generalized muscle rigidity, rhabdomyolysis, and hyperkalemia minutes after receiving halothane and succinylcholine during surgery. Dantrolene treats this crisis by blocking which channel?
options: Sarcolemmal nicotinic acetylcholine receptor
T-tubule dihydropyridine receptor (CaV1.1)
Cardiac ryanodine receptor (RyR2)
Sarcoplasmic reticulum ryanodine receptor (RyR1)
questions.explain: Malignant hyperthermia is triggered by volatile anesthetics or succinylcholine in patients with RYR1 mutations causing uncontrolled SR Ca2+ release; dantrolene binds RyR1 to inhibit further calcium release.

open.q: Name the sarcoplasmic reticulum calcium channel inhibited by dantrolene in the treatment of malignant hyperthermia.

questions.q: Which ATP-dependent pump sequesters cytosolic calcium back into the sarcoplasmic reticulum lumen to allow skeletal muscle relaxation?
options: SERCA, the sarco/endoplasmic reticulum Ca2+-ATPase
Na+/K+-ATPase, the plasma membrane sodium pump
H+/K+-ATPase, the gastric parietal proton pump
F-type ATP synthase, the mitochondrial rotary motor
questions.explain: SERCA pumps two Ca2+ ions back into the sarcoplasmic reticulum per ATP hydrolyzed, lowering cytosolic Ca2+ so it dissociates from troponin C and tropomyosin re-blocks actin.

open.q: Name the ATP-driven pump that transports calcium from the sarcoplasm back into the sarcoplasmic reticulum during muscle relaxation.

questions.q: How does smooth muscle initiate contraction in response to elevated intracellular calcium, given that it lacks troponin?
options: Calcium binds directly to actin filaments and exposes myosin sites
Calcium binds calmodulin, activating MLCK to phosphorylate myosin light chains
Calcium activates troponin C-like subunits on smooth muscle tropomyosin
Calcium directly inhibits myosin light-chain phosphatase
questions.explain: Smooth muscle lacks troponin; Ca2+ binds calmodulin, forming a Ca2+-calmodulin complex that activates MLCK to phosphorylate the 20-kDa regulatory light chain of myosin II, enabling cross-bridge cycling.

open.q: Name the enzyme activated by the calcium-calmodulin complex to initiate smooth muscle contraction.

questions.q: How does nitric oxide (NO) induce relaxation of vascular smooth muscle?
options: Activates adenylyl cyclase to inhibit SERCA calcium reuptake
Blocks voltage-gated potassium channels to depolarize the cell
Activates guanylyl cyclase and PKG, stimulating myosin light-chain phosphatase
Directly phosphorylates troponin I to block actin binding
questions.explain: NO increases cGMP and activates protein kinase G (PKG), which activates myosin light-chain phosphatase (MLCP) to dephosphorylate myosin light chains and lowers cytosolic Ca2+, relaxing smooth muscle.

open.q: Which phosphatase is stimulated by protein kinase G to dephosphorylate myosin light chains and relax smooth muscle?

questions.q: What is the 'latch state' characteristic of tonic smooth muscle contraction?
options: Permanent cross-bridge locking caused by intracellular ATP depletion
Rapid cycling of unphosphorylated myosin heads along actin
Calcium-independent activation of troponin T in the thin filament
MLCP dephosphorylates attached myosin heads, sustaining force at low ATP cost
questions.explain: In the latch state, MLCP dephosphorylates myosin light chains while myosin is still bound to actin, markedly slowing detachment so tonic force is sustained with very low ATP expenditure.

open.q: What term describes the energy-efficient state in smooth muscle where dephosphorylated cross-bridges remain attached to maintain sustained tone?

questions.q: Which enzyme catalyzes the reversible transfer of a high-energy phosphate group from phosphocreatine to ADP to rapidly regenerate ATP during the first few seconds of intense sprint exercise?
options: Creatine kinase
Adenylate kinase
Pyruvate kinase
Phosphoglycerate kinase
questions.explain: Creatine kinase (CK-MM in skeletal muscle) transfers phosphate from phosphocreatine to ADP, providing immediate ATP buffering before glycolysis and oxidative phosphorylation ramp up.

open.q: Name the enzyme that transfers a high-energy phosphate from phosphocreatine to ADP to rapidly replenish ATP in contracting muscle.

questions.q: Which muscle enzyme catalyzes the conversion of two ADP molecules into one ATP and one AMP during intense exercise when ATP demand outpaces supply?
options: Adenylate kinase
Creatine phosphokinase
AMP deaminase
Pyruvate carboxylase
questions.explain: Adenylate kinase (myokinase) catalyzes 2 ADP <-> ATP + AMP; the resulting rise in AMP allosterically activates phosphofructokinase-1 and glycogen phosphorylase b to boost ATP generation.

open.q: Name the enzyme that converts two molecules of ADP into one ATP and one AMP in exercising skeletal muscle.

questions.q: Which monomeric heme protein in Type I (slow-twitch) skeletal and cardiac muscle stores oxygen and facilitates intracellular oxygen diffusion to mitochondria?
options: Hemoglobin A
Neuroglobin
Myoglobin
Cytochrome c
questions.explain: Myoglobin is a single-polypeptide globin with a hyperbolic oxygen dissociation curve and a much lower P50 (~2.8 mmHg) than hemoglobin, releasing O2 to mitochondria during intense muscle work.

open.q: Name the monomeric oxygen-binding heme protein abundant in red slow-twitch skeletal and cardiac muscle fibers.

questions.q: How do Type I (slow oxidative) skeletal muscle fibers differ biochemically from Type IIb/IIx (fast glycolytic) fibers?
options: Type I fibers have higher myosin ATPase activity and fewer mitochondria
Type I fibers rely predominantly on anaerobic glycogenolysis
Type I fibers contain less myoglobin and lower capillary density
Type I fibers are high in myoglobin and mitochondria with slow ATPase
questions.explain: Type I (red) fibers are fatigue-resistant endurance fibers rich in myoglobin, capillaries, and mitochondria for aerobic fatty acid and glucose oxidation, whereas Type IIb (white) fibers rely on rapid anaerobic glycolysis and fast myosin ATPase.

open.q: Which skeletal muscle fiber type is characterized by high myoglobin content, abundant mitochondria, slow myosin ATPase activity, and high fatigue resistance?

questions.q: During prolonged moderate-intensity aerobic exercise, how does skeletal muscle fuel utilization shift over time?
options: Shifts from glycogen and blood glucose toward plasma free fatty acids
Shifts exclusively to amino acid oxidation within the first ten minutes
Relies solely on phosphocreatine stores throughout a full marathon
Switches from fatty acids to anaerobic lactate production
questions.explain: Initial exercise consumes phosphocreatine and muscle glycogen, but as duration extends beyond 30-60 minutes, epinephrine and falling insulin stimulate lipolysis, making plasma free fatty acids the dominant aerobic fuel.

open.q: What becomes the primary energy substrate oxidized by skeletal muscle during prolonged submaximal endurance exercise?

questions.q: In the glucose-alanine (Cahill) cycle, why does exercising skeletal muscle export amino nitrogen to the liver as alanine rather than free ammonia?
options: Free ammonia cannot cross skeletal muscle capillary walls
Alanine safely carries nitrogen from BCAA transamination to the liver
Skeletal muscle contains a complete functional urea cycle
Alanine directly stimulates hepatic glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis
questions.explain: Muscle lacks urea cycle enzymes; transaminating pyruvate with glutamate forms non-toxic alanine, which travels to the liver to be converted back into glucose (for muscle) and urea (for renal excretion).

open.q: Name the amino acid synthesized in skeletal muscle via transamination of pyruvate to transport nitrogen safely to the liver.

questions.q: A 32-year-old man is rescued after being trapped under collapsed concrete for 8 hours and develops dark brown urine, acute kidney injury, hyperkalemia, and a serum creatine kinase of 85,000 U/L. Which heme protein released from damaged myocytes causes acute tubular necrosis?
options: Hemoglobin
Haptoglobin
Myoglobin
Ceruloplasmin
questions.explain: Crush injury causes rhabdomyolysis, releasing massive amounts of myoglobin into plasma; filtered myoglobin precipitates in renal tubules and generates free radicals, causing pigment-induced acute tubular necrosis.

open.q: Name the muscle heme protein released during rhabdomyolysis that precipitates in renal tubules and causes acute kidney injury.

questions.q: Why does cardiac muscle troponin I (cTnI) provide greater diagnostic specificity for myocardial infarction than total serum creatine kinase (CK)?
options: Total CK is more specific to myocardium because skeletal muscle contains little creatine kinase
cTnI is released earlier after myocardial injury and returns to baseline sooner than total CK
Total CK is restricted to cardiomyocytes, whereas cTnI is also abundant in skeletal muscle
cTnI is a cardiac-specific isoform, whereas total CK can also rise after skeletal muscle injury
questions.explain: Because skeletal muscle contains abundant CK-MM (and small amounts of CK-MB), skeletal muscle injury elevates total CK, whereas cardiac troponin I has an amino acid sequence unique to myocardium.

open.q: Which cardiac regulatory protein is the gold-standard serum biomarker for myocardial necrosis due to its exclusive expression in cardiomyocytes?

questions.q: A patient with myasthenia gravis develops fatigable skeletal muscle weakness due to antibodies against postsynaptic nicotinic acetylcholine receptors. Which event is directly reduced at the motor end plate?
options: End-plate depolarisation reaching threshold for a muscle action potential
Release of calcium from the sarcoplasmic reticulum by every action potential
Binding of oxygen to myoglobin
ATP synthesis by mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation
questions.explain: Loss of functional postsynaptic nicotinic receptors reduces the end-plate potential, making it less likely to reach threshold and trigger a muscle action potential.

questions.q: A patient develops muscle rigidity after exposure to a drug that causes uncontrolled calcium release from skeletal-muscle sarcoplasmic reticulum. Which channel is primarily implicated in malignant hyperthermia?
options: Ryanodine receptor type 1 (RyR1)
Dihydropyridine receptor in the T-tubule as the calcium-release pore
Sarcolemmal voltage-gated sodium channel
SERCA calcium ATPase as the calcium-release channel
questions.explain: Malignant hyperthermia is commonly associated with abnormal RyR1-mediated calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum, producing sustained contraction and hypermetabolism.

questions.q: Dantrolene is administered during malignant hyperthermia. Which biochemical process does it reduce?
options: Calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum through RyR1
Calcium binding to troponin C
Acetylcholine synthesis in motor neurons
ATP binding to myosin heads
questions.explain: Dantrolene reduces calcium release through skeletal-muscle ryanodine receptors, lowering cytosolic calcium and muscle contracture.

questions.q: A patient with severe hypocalcaemia develops carpopedal spasm. Which change in excitable tissue helps explain the increased neuromuscular excitability?
options: Reduced extracellular calcium lowers the threshold for voltage-gated sodium channel activation
Increased extracellular calcium prevents sodium channel opening
Reduced intracellular potassium blocks all action potentials
Increased acetylcholinesterase activity prolongs end-plate depolarisation
questions.explain: Low extracellular calcium increases the excitability of nerve membranes, in part by lowering the threshold for voltage-gated sodium channel activation.

questions.q: A patient with an inherited defect of muscle glycogen phosphorylase develops exercise-induced cramps and fails to increase blood lactate during forearm exercise. Which disorder is most likely?
options: McArdle disease
Pompe disease
Duchenne muscular dystrophy
Myasthenia gravis
questions.explain: McArdle disease (glycogen storage disease type V) is caused by muscle glycogen phosphorylase deficiency, impairing glycogenolysis and the rise in lactate during exercise.
